tabernacle.e: From Middle English tabernacle (14th century), from Old French tabernacle, from Latin tabernāculum (“tent, booth, shed”), the diminutive of taberna (“hut, shed”). By surface analysis, taberna + -cle.
tabernacle.g: Any temporary dwelling; a hut, tent, or booth.

table.e: From Middle English table, tabel, tabil, tabul, from Old English tabele, tabul, tablu, tabule, tabula (“board”); also as tæfl, tæfel, an early Germanic borrowing of Latin tabula (“tablet, board, plank, chart”). The sense of “piece of furniture” is from Old French table, of same Latin origin; Old English used bēod or bord instead for this meaning: see board.
table.g: Furniture with a top surface to accommodate a variety of uses.

tablet.e: From Middle English tablet, from Old French tablete (Modern French tablette), diminutive of table (“table”).
tablet.g: A slab of clay, stone or wood used for inscription.

tabor.e: From Middle English, from Old French tabour, from Arabic طُنْبُور (ṭunbūr), ultimately from the Middle Persian ancestor of Classical Persian تنبور (tanbūr).
From various Slavic languages, from a Turkic language.
tabor.g: A military train of men and wagons; an encampment of such resources.

tackle.e: From Middle English takel (“gear, apparatus”), from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German takel (“ship's rigging”), perhaps related to Middle Dutch taken (“to grasp, seize”).
tackle.g: A device for grasping an object and an attached means of moving it, as a rope and hook.

tact.e: Borrowed from French tact, following a semantic shift from earlier tact (“sense of touch; feeling”), borrowed from Latin tāctus (“touched”). The borrowing was likely influenced by earlier English tact (“sense of touch; feeling”), which was a parallel borrowing directly from the Latin.
tact.g: Sensitive mental touch; special skill or faculty; keen perception or discernment; ready power of appreciating and doing what is required by

tail.e: From Middle English tail, taile, taille, tayil, tayl, tayle, tayll, teil, tæȝel, from Old English tæġel, tæġl (“tail”), from Proto-West Germanic *tagl, from Proto-Germanic *taglą (“hair, fiber; hair of a tail”), from Proto-Indo-European *doḱ- (“hair of the tail”), from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- (“to tear, fray, shred”).
tail.g: The caudal appendage of an animal that is attached to their posterior and near the anus or cloaca.

tail.e: From Anglo-Norman, probably from a shortened form of entail.

taint.e: From Middle French teint, from Old French teint (past participle of teindre (“to dye, to tinge”)), from Latin tinctum (past participle of tingere); compare tint.
taint.g: A contamination, decay or putrefaction, especially in food.

taint.e: From Middle English taynt, aphetic form of attaynt, atteynt, from Old French atteinte (“a blow, stroke”).
taint.g: A thrust with a lance, which fails of its intended effect.

take.e: From Middle English taken (“to take, lay hold of, grasp, strike”), from Old English tacan (“to grasp, touch”), probably of North Germanic origin, from Old Norse taka (“to touch, take”). Alternatively, inherited from Proto-West Germanic *takan (“to take; grasp, touch”). Both from Proto-Germanic *tēkaną (“to touch”).
take.g: To get into one's hands, possession, or control, with or without force.

taken.e: From Middle English taken, takenn, from Old English tacen, *ġetacen, from Old Norse tekinn, from Proto-Germanic *tēkanaz, past participle of Proto-Germanic *tēkaną (“to take; grasp; touch”). Morphologically take + -n.
taken.g: Infatuated; fond of or attracted to.

taker.e: From Middle English takere, equivalent to take + -er.

tale.e: From Middle English tale, from Old English talu (“tale, series, calculation”), from Proto-West Germanic *talu, from Proto-Germanic *talō (“calculation, number”), from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“to reckon, count”).
tale.g: A rehearsal of what has occurred; narrative; discourse; statement; history; story.

tale.e: From Middle English talen, from Old English talian (“to count, calculate, reckon”), from Proto-West Germanic *talōn, from Proto-Germanic *talōną (“to count”), from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“to count, reckon, aim, calculate, adjust”).

talebearer.e: From Middle English taleberer; equivalent to tale + bearer.
talebearer.g: An indiscreet person who spreads gossip or blame.

talent.e: From Middle English talent, from Old English talente, borrowed from the plural of Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money”), from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance, a particular weight, especially of gold, sum of money, a talent”).
talent.g: A marked natural ability or skill.

tales.g: A person available to fill vacancies in a jury.

talk.e: From Middle English talken, talkien, from Old English *tealcian (“to talk, chat”), from Proto-West Germanic *talkōn, from Proto-Germanic *talkōną (“to talk, chatter”), frequentative form of Proto-Germanic *talōną (“to count, recount, tell”), from Proto-Indo-European *dol-, *del- (“to aim, calculate, adjust, count”), equivalent to tell + -k.
talk.g: To communicate, usually by means of speech.

talk.e: From Middle English talk, talke (“conversation; discourse”), from the verb (see above).
talk.g: A conversation or discussion; usually serious, but informal.

talker.e: From Middle English talkere, equivalent to talk + -er.
talker.g: A person who talks, especially one who gives a speech, or is loquacious or garrulous.

talking.e: From Middle English talkyng, talkynge. By surface analysis, talk + -ing.

tall.e: From Middle English tall, talle, tal (“seemly, becoming, handsome, good-looking, excellent, good, valiant, lively in speech, bold, great, large, big”), from Old English *tæl, ġetæl (“swift, ready, having mastery of”), from Proto-Germanic *talaz (“submissive, pliable, obedient”), from Proto-Indo-European *dol-, *del- (“to aim, calculate, adjust, reckon”).
tall.g: Having a top that is far up (contrast: deep ('having a bottom that is far down' ).)

tamarisk.e: From Late Latin tamariscus, from Latin tamarix.
tamarisk.g: Any of several shrubs, of the genus Tamarix, native to arid regions in Eurasia and Africa, often invasive in other arid regions.

tambourine.e: From French tambourin (“little drum”), from French tambour (“drum”). Ultimately from Arabic طُنْبُور (ṭunbūr); see it and Persian تنبور for more.
tambourine.g: A percussion instrument consisting of a small, usually wooden, hoop closed on one side with a drum frame and featuring jingling metal disks

tame.e: From Middle English tame, tome, weak inflection forms of Middle English tam, tom, from Old English tam, tom (“domesticated, tame”), from Proto-West Germanic *tam (“tame”), from Proto-Germanic *tamaz (“brought into the home, tame”), from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂- (“to tame, dominate”).
From Middle English tamen (“to cut into, broach”).
tame.g: To broach or enter upon; to taste, as a liquor; to divide; to distribute; to deal out.

tanner.e: From Middle English tannere, from Old English tannere; and Old French tannour, equivalent to tan + -er.
tanner.g: A person whose occupation is to tan hides, or convert them into leather by the use of tan.

tanner.e: Named after John Sigismund Tanner (1705–1775), who designed a sixpence for the Royal Mint during the reign of King George II.
tanner.g: A former British coin worth six old pence.

tap.e: Verb etymology 1, verb sense 1.3.5 (“to turn over (a playing card or playing piece) to remind players that it has already been used in that round”) alludes to the abilities or resources of the card or piece having been drawn on to the point of temporary exhaustion: see verb etymology 1, verb sense 1.3.2.
tap.g: A conical peg or pin used to close and open the hole or vent in a container.

tap.e: Verb etymology 2, verb sense 1.1.1 (“to arrest (someone)”) and etymology 2, verb sense 1.6 (“to choose or designate (someone) for a duty, etc.”) allude to a police officer or other person tapping someone on their shoulder to catch their attention or to select them.
tap.g: To strike (someone or something), chiefly lightly with a clear sound, but sometimes hard.

tapestry.e: From Middle English tapestrie, from Old French tapisserie (“tapestry”), from Ancient Greek τάπης (tápēs), from an Iranian source.
tapestry.g: A heavy woven cloth, often with decorative pictorial designs, normally hung on walls.

tar.e: From Middle English ter, terr, tarr, from Old English teoru, from Proto-West Germanic *teru, from Proto-Germanic *terwą, from Proto-Indo-European *derwo-, from *dóru (“tree”).
tar.g: A black, oil, sticky, viscous substance, consisting mainly of hydrocarbons derived from organic materials such as wood, peat, or coal.
A program for archiving files, common on Unix systems.

tare.e: From Middle English tare (“vetch”), from Old English *taru, from Proto-West Germanic *taru.
tare.g: A vetch, or the seed of a vetch (genus Vicia, esp. Vicia sativa).

tare.e: Borrowed from Middle French tare, from Italian tara, from Arabic طَرْحَة (ṭarḥa, “that which is thrown away”), a derivative of طَرَحَ (ṭaraḥa, “to throw (away)”).
tare.g: The empty weight of a container; unladen weight.

target.e: From Middle French targette, targuete, diminutive of targe (“light shield”), from Old French, from Frankish *targa (“buckler”), akin to Old Norse targa (“small round shield”) (whence also Old English targe, targa (“shield”)) from Proto-Germanic *targǭ (“edge”), from Proto-Indo-European *derǵʰ- (“fenced lot”).
target.g: A butt or mark to shoot at, as for practice, or to test the accuracy of a firearm, or the force of a projectile.

tarnish.e: From Middle English ternysshen, from Old French terniss-, stem of ternir (“to make dim, make wan”), borrowed from Old High German *ternen, tarnen, from Proto-West Germanic *darnijan (“to conceal”).
tarnish.g: Oxidation or discoloration, especially of a decorative metal exposed to air.

tarry.e: From Middle English tarien, terien (“to vex, harass, cause to hesitate, delay”), from Old English tirian, tirġan, terġan (“to worry, exasperate, pain, provoke, excite”), from Proto-Germanic *terganą, *targijaną (“to pull, tease, irritate”), from Proto-Indo-European *derHgʰ- (“to pull, tug, irritate”).
tarry.g: To delay; to be late or tardy in beginning or doing anything.

tarry.e: From Middle English terrie, equivalent to tar + -y.

task.e: From Middle English taske (“task, tax”), from Old Northern French tasque, (compare Old French variant tasche), from Medieval Latin tasca, alteration of taxa, from Latin taxō (“to censure; to charge”).
task.g: A piece of work done as part of one’s duties.

taskmaster.g: Someone who supervises workers, especially one who imposes hard or burdensome work.

tassel.e: From Middle English tassel, from Old French tassel, from Latin tāxillus (“small cube”), from tālus (“ankle”).
tassel.g: A ball-shaped bunch of plaited or otherwise entangled threads from which at one end protrudes a cord on which the ball is hung, and which ma

taste.e: The noun came from the verb, and the two conflated after English lost its infinitive suffix -en, though tasten was most likely already used nominatively (as a gerund), similar to Modern English tasting. Almost fully displaced native smack, from Middle English smac, smak, smacke, from Old English smæc, smæċċ (“taste, smatch”).
taste.g: One of the sensations produced by the tongue in response to certain chemicals; the quality of giving this sensation.

tasting.e: From Middle English tastinge, taastynge, equivalent to taste + -ing (present participle ending).

tasty.e: From taste + -y. The Philippine sense is due to a genericized trademark from Taystee Bread Company, a defunct American company.
tasty.g: Having a pleasant or satisfying flavor.

tattoo.e: From earlier tattaow, tattow, a borrowing from a Polynesian language, e.g. Samoan tatau (“tattoo; to tap, to strike”).
tattoo.g: An image made on a body part, usually the skin with ink and a needle.

tattoo.e: From earlier tap-to, borrowed from Dutch taptoe, from tap (“tap; faucet on a cask”) + toe (“to; shut”).
tattoo.g: A signal played five minutes before taps (lights out).

taunt.e: From Middle French tanter (“to tempt, try, provoke”), variant of Old French tempter (“to try”).
taunt.g: To make fun of (someone); to goad (a person) into responding, often in an aggressive manner.

tavern.e: From Middle English taverne, from Old French taverne (“wine shop”), from Latin taberna (“inn”).

tax.e: From Middle English taxe, from Middle French taxe, from Medieval Latin taxa, from Latin taxō (“to appraise, value, estimate; (medieval) to tax”).
tax.g: Money or goods collected by a government (or an entity to whom the government has delegated this power, e.g. in tax farming) to fund itself

tax.e: From Middle English taxen, from Anglo-Norman taxer (“to impose a tax”), from Latin taxāre (“to handle, to censure, to appraise, to compute”).
tax.g: To impose and collect a tax from (a person or company).

taxation.e: From Middle English taxacioun, from Anglo-Norman taxacion, from Latin taxātio (“rating, appraisal”). By surface analysis, tax + -ation.
taxation.g: The act of imposing taxes and the fact of being taxed.

teach.e: From Middle English techen, from Old English tǣċan (“to show, declare, demonstrate; teach, instruct, train; assign, prescribe, direct; warn; persuade”), from Proto-West Germanic *taikijan, from Proto-Germanic *taikijaną (“to show”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show”).
